rows.context: With Hitsman, conscription as a national divide.

Histories of the King government at war (1975), conscription (with J. M. Hitsman, 1977) and the federal mandarinate (1982); co-author of a survey of Canada's external relations (1994). His 1998 polemic belongs to The 'Who Killed Canadian History?' debate.
rows.works: Canada's War (1975); Broken Promises (1977); The Ottawa Men (1982); Empire to Umpire (1994, with Hillmer)

rows.context: Carried the charge to a public audience: academic historians had abandoned a national past for "overspecialized and ideologically driven forms of history" (as summarized by McKillop). Book unread.

verification.note: Abstract read: Granatstein "miscasts the role of the scholar as citizen, misrepresents the purpose of scholarship, and distorts the nature and quality of academic historical writing"; his narrow national history is itself "part of the process of political legitimation". Checked against: Crossref DOI record; OpenAlex abstract. Same work also checked as cdng_mckillop_1999 (supporting_page_checked, 2026-10-12; who_killed_debate): Abstract read: Granatstein "accuses Canadian academic historians of having abandoned the writing of a national past in favour of overspecialized and ideologically driven forms of history"; McKillop argues he miscasts the scholar as citizen, puts forward a national history no better suited to national self-understanding, which "can be viewed instead as part of the process of political legitimation", and ignores that "event-driven facts are inseparable from considerations of value". Checked against: Crossref DOI record (pp. 269–300); abstract via OpenAlex.
